    Scaling laws for a calculator: parameters, data, and where it stops

    Follow-up to the 14-level benchmark and the generalisation follow-up. The question this time: if the model and the data are scaled up, does performance follow, is there an asymptote, or can it just keep going? One task, one architecture family, three knobs turned one at a time: parameters, training length, and the number of distinct problems in the training pool.

  3. Nov 16, 2026 · 11 min read

    Does the calculator generalise? Gaps, a wider pool, and a procedure for sine

    Follow-up to the harder benchmark, which ended with a model that scores 97.7% inside the sizes it trained on, 27% one size beyond them, and knows sine as a table of 1,999 values. The question left open there was whether these models generalise at all. Three tests, run as one fine-tune: leave sizes out in the middle of the range, widen the range and test past the new edge, and replace the sine table with a procedure.

  4. Nov 15, 2026 · Updated Nov 16, 2026 · 28 min read

    A calculator benchmark that takes longer to saturate

    Follow-up to the calculator at 99%. That benchmark is used up: seven levels, 99.1% exact match. The ask this time was harder and harder problems, equations included, and an eval that takes longer to saturate. Same small transformer, same recipe (a supervised thinking block before the answer), 14 levels instead of 7, and worked solutions of up to 2,300 tokens.

  5. Nov 14, 2026 · Updated Nov 15, 2026 · 29 min read

    A calculator LLM at 99%: the scratchpad mattered more than the weights

    Follow-up to the thinking-token ablation, which left the calculator at 83.3% exact match. The ask was to scale it out to 95%+, with more weights and whatever architecture changes help. Same task, same 14,000 held-out test problems, same display rule (integers in full, otherwise 4 significant digits). It ends at 99.1%, and most of the distance was not covered by weights.

  6. Nov 14, 2026 · 22 min read

    Should a transformer say "um"? A calculator LLM and a thinking-token ablation

    A 3-million-parameter transformer is taught a calculator, from 47+85 up to sin(1.2) and the quadratic formula. Then 32 training runs compare ways for it to think before it answers: filler tokens, discrete and continuous thinking tokens, looped layers, scratchpads. Every number below is measured on those runs (one H100, 20,000 steps each, 14,000 held-out test problems).
